network.overall_strategy: This is a complete conditional research network, not a demonstrated synthesis of tryptophan from simple terrestrial feedstocks. The supplied literature does not establish ten validated prebiotic pathways. Accordingly, the ten pathways below are distinct directed routes through four terminal reaction families; some differ only in precursor processing. Indole, indole-3-acetaldehyde and indole-3-pyruvate are explicitly declared boundary feedstocks whose geochemical availability remains unresolved. No unsupported aqueous indole synthesis or incorrectly connected indole-plus-pyruvate coupling is inserted. Wang et al. (2024) support indole formation in irradiated 5 K ice, not its formation in the terrestrial environments represented here. Every numerical protocol below is a proposed screening window unless explicitly described otherwise; these specifications do not constitute measured yields, published optima or integrated validation. Strong-base hydantoin processing and pyridoxal-metal catalysis are laboratory comparators, not established prebiotic processes. All experiments are anoxic, with UV shielding except during the controlled photocatalytic screen. Proposed fractionation and solution-conditioning operations require measured recovery and are not assumed to occur naturally. Product identification requires authentic-standard chromatography, mass spectrometry, isotope tracing where appropriate, and substrate/product survival controls. Neutral-parent formulas represent pH-dependent aqueous species; protonation equilibria and spectator counterions are implicit. Stoichiometric molecule IDs are never repeated; important coefficients are explained in mechanisms. The restricted role vocabulary uses intermediate for coproducts, and environment_formed gives one representative setting rather than an exclusive provenance. No enantioselectivity or numerical formation yield is assumed.

reactions.name: Direct Strecker entry from supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed initial concentrations: aldehyde 0.1-1 mM, total ammonia 50-200 mM, total cyanide 5-20 mM; pH 8.0-9.0; sample over 1-48 h. Use a shaded, anoxic aqueous compartment. Quantify cyanohydrin, aminonitrile and aldehyde loss separately. Before subsequent heating, isolate a quantified aminonitrile fraction by a laboratory separation and reconstitute it; neither quantitative recovery nor a natural separation mechanism is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, followed by reversible imine formation and cyanide addition at the imine carbon. The aldehyde carbon becomes the amino-bearing carbon, and the cyanide carbon becomes the eventual carboxyl carbon. Water is the net coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Reaction-class support exists for Strecker synthesis, but this substrate-specific implementation is not established by the supplied studies. Wang et al. (2024) motivate an indolic precursor route without demonstrating this terrestrial sequence. The scarcity of aromatic amino acids in standard inventories discussed by Mojarro et al. (2025) is not a conservation objection to using a supplied indolic aldehyde. The decisive limitations are aldehyde provenance, competing condensation and unmeasured productive selectivity.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrolysis of tryptophan aminonitrile
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline water; hydrolysis promoter, not a mineral-specific catalyst

conditions.other: Proposed aminonitrile concentration 0.1-1 mM; initial pH measured at 298 K of 9.5-11.0; residence-time screen 6-168 h. Exclude oxygen and light. Use a free-cyanide-depleted input fraction rather than directly heating an uncharacterized Strecker mixture. Cool aliquots to 303 K or below, adjust to pH 6-7, and quantify residual nitrile, amide, tryptophan and degradation products. Useful conversion at this moderate alkalinity is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis produce the amino acid and ammonia. Two water molecules are consumed per aminonitrile; mol_004 is therefore listed only once despite its inferred coefficient of two.
reactions.reasoning: This is a class-supported but substrate-unvalidated completion of the Strecker proposal discussed by Wang et al. (2024). Alkaline rather than strongly acidic processing is chosen to avoid a known vulnerability of indolic amino acids during harsh acid treatment. No supplied paper establishes this hydrolysis window, its yield or tryptophan survival. Guo et al. (2019) demonstrate destruction at much higher temperatures, not safety throughout the proposed lower-temperature window.

reactions.name: Reversible cyanohydrin trapping of indole-3-acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Proposed aldehyde concentration 0.1-1 mM and total cyanide 5-20 mM; pH 8.0-8.8; sample over 0.5-24 h. Omit added ammonia during this diagnostic trapping stage. Keep shaded and anoxic. Transfer to rxn_004 without heating after measuring the aldehyde/cyanohydrin distribution.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible cyanide addition to the aldehyde carbonyl followed by proton transfer forms the cyanohydrin. The reaction stores, rather than constructs, the required indolic aldehyde skeleton.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific implementation: ordinary aldehyde-cyanohydrin chemistry justifies testing the equilibrium, but the supplied literature contains no measured equilibrium constant or yield for this substrate under these conditions. This route is included as a potentially relevant reservoir feeding Strecker chemistry, not as an independent solution to indole-3-acetaldehyde formation.

reactions.name: Ammonia-driven cyanohydrin equilibration into the Strecker aminonitrile

conditions.other: Use the quantified rxn_003 mixture; adjust total ammonia to 50-200 mM and pH to 8.0-9.0. Proposed residence time 6-72 h. Maintain anoxia and shading. Measure aminonitrile accumulation rather than inferring conversion from cyanohydrin disappearance. Apply the same product-isolation and recovery checks required after rxn_001.

reactions.mechanism: The cyanohydrin first equilibrates with aldehyde and cyanide. Aldehyde then forms an imine with ammonia, and cyanide traps that imine. The net equation releases water; it is not direct displacement of an unactivated hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific implementation grounded in reversible cyanohydrin and Strecker chemistry. No supplied paper demonstrates that this indolic cyanohydrin feeds the aminonitrile at a useful rate. Its merit is as an alternative kinetic entry into the same Strecker module; cyanohydrin stabilization could instead suppress productive flux.

reactions.name: Candidate aminonitrile-to-hydantoin carbon dioxide trapping

conditions.pressure: 1 bar in a covered aqueous compartment
conditions.other: Proposed aminonitrile concentration 0.1-1 mM; total dissolved inorganic carbon 50-250 mM; pH 8.5-9.5; residence time 12-96 h. Carbon dioxide is represented by mol_007, including its bicarbonate/carbonate forms at the stated pH. Quantify inorganic-carbon speciation and ammonia carried from the preceding step. Maintain anoxia and shading; do not infer hydantoin formation from loss of aminonitrile.

reactions.mechanism: A Bucherer-Bergs-type sequence would combine amino-group carbamylation with nitrile conversion and intramolecular cyclization to the hydantoin. Water can participate in elementary steps but is not consumed in the balanced net aminonitrile-plus-carbon-dioxide transformation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative within the supplied evidence: conventional hydantoin chemistry motivates this trapping branch, but no supplied study establishes its operation with this indolic aminonitrile. Dissolved inorganic-carbon speciation, competing hydrolysis and cyclization kinetics are explicit bottlenecks. The branch tests chemical persistence and downstream release; it does not improve the unresolved aldehyde supply.

reactions.name: Laboratory hydantoin ring-opening comparator
agents: Sodium hydroxide as an externally supplied laboratory hydrolysis promoter

conditions.other: Proposed hydantoin concentration 0.1-1 mM and NaOH concentration 0.1-0.5 M; residence time 2-24 h. Exclude oxygen and light. Follow ring opening, direct amino-acid release and indolic decomposition separately. Transfer only a quantified N-carbamoyltryptophan fraction to rxn_007. These alkaline conditions are laboratory comparators, not an asserted evaporitic-pool composition.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-promoted hydrolysis opens the hydantoin ring to an N-carbamoyl amino acid. One water molecule is consumed in the neutral-parent net equation; base consumption associated with product ionization is handled by the stated pH reservoir.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific laboratory comparator: the supplied research does not validate ring opening of this indolic hydantoin or demonstrate accumulation of N-carbamoyltryptophan under a prebiotic regime. Explicit base loading and time-temperature screening replace an unsupported assumption of useful uncatalyzed hydrolysis. Product survival and separation remain necessary measurements.

reactions.name: Laboratory N-carbamoyltryptophan hydrolysis comparator
agents: Sodium hydroxide as an externally supplied laboratory hydrolysis promoter

conditions.other: Proposed N-carbamoyltryptophan concentration 0.1-1 mM and NaOH concentration 0.5-2 M; residence time 1-24 h. Maintain anoxia and darkness. Cool to 303 K or below before analytical neutralization. Measure tryptophan recovery against a tryptophan-only survival control exposed to the same conditions. Carbon dioxide will occur primarily as dissolved carbonate species during alkaline processing.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the carbamoyl group releases tryptophan, ammonia and inorganic carbon. One water molecule is consumed in the neutral-parent net equation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific laboratory comparator: no supplied paper establishes this deprotection step, its rate or a natural source of the required strong alkalinity. It is separated from hydantoin opening because the two transformations need not share a useful operating window. A chemically balanced endpoint does not establish selective tryptophan recovery.

reactions.name: Candidate Fe(II)-hydroxide-mediated reductive amination
agents: Mixed Fe(II)/Fe(III) hydroxide interface, with Fe(OH)2 as a consumable reductant
Anoxically supplied ferric oxyhydroxide seed; no molecular oxygen used

conditions.other: Proposed indole-3-pyruvate concentration 0.05-0.2 mM and total ammonia 50-200 mM. Prepare 5-20 mM Fe(II) with an equal molar amount of initially supplied Fe(III), targeting an initial Fe(II):Fe(III) ratio of 1:1. Initial pH at 298 K: 9.0-10.5; sample over 1-48 h. Ferric material must be supplied from an inherited mineral or anoxic salt preparation rather than oxygen exposure. Exclude sulfide from this diagnostic branch. Rapidly cool and separate solids before product analysis; characterize iron oxidation states and phases before and after reaction.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or related adsorbed intermediate at the keto group, followed by a two-electron reduction. The formal net reaction consumes two Fe(OH)2 units and produces two FeOOH units plus one water molecule per tryptophan. FeOOH is an idealized ferric product composition, not a prediction of a particular crystalline phase.
reactions.reasoning: Analogue-supported hypothesis, not a demonstrated indole-3-pyruvate reaction. Huber and Wachtershauser (2003) support iron-mediated reductive amination of alpha-keto acids; Barge et al. (2019) support alkaline mixed-valence iron systems and report maximal alanine formation near a 1:1 Fe(II):Fe(III) ratio. Neither supplied result establishes this indolic substrate, the proposed window or the formal FeOOH endpoint. Competing keto-group reduction, indole-3-pyruvate degradation and initial ferric-mineral availability must be assessed.

reactions.name: Candidate pyritization-coupled reductive amination
agents: Mackinawite surface; FeS and dissolved sulfide are consumable redox reagents

conditions.other: Proposed indole-3-pyruvate concentration 0.05-0.2 mM, total ammonia 50-200 mM, freshly characterized FeS 1-10 g/L, and total dissolved sulfide 1-10 mM. Initial pH at 298 K: 8.0-9.0; residence-time screen 6-168 h. Maintain anoxia and darkness. Measure dissolved sulfide, gas formation, FeS-to-FeS2 conversion and organic products independently. Pyrite formation alone is not an acceptance criterion for amino-acid synthesis.

reactions.mechanism: The proposed coupling reduces a keto-acid-derived imine while sulfide sulfur is oxidized to the disulfide state during FeS2 formation. FeS plus H2S formally supplies the required two reducing equivalents, with water as the organic condensation coproduct. Whether those electrons actually reach the indolic imine is unresolved.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative mechanistic coupling with related reaction-class precedent from Huber and Wachtershauser (2003). The supplied findings do not establish indole-3-pyruvate conversion or prove that pyritization powers its reductive amination. Low-temperature pyrite kinetics, competing hydrogen evolution and substrate degradation can prevent productive coupling despite a balanced net equation. This branch must not be assigned demonstrated flux.

reactions.name: Candidate formate-fed pyrite photoreductive amination
agents: Naturally occurring pyrite as a candidate semiconductor photocatalyst

conditions.other: Proposed indole-3-pyruvate concentration 0.05-0.2 mM, total ammonia 50-200 mM, formate 10-100 mM, and pyrite loading 0.5-5 g/L; pH 8.5-9.5. Diagnostic irradiation: 365 ± 10 nm, incident irradiance 1-5 mW/cm2, optical path 1-2 mm, duration 1-24 h. Use dark, no-pyrite, no-formate and tryptophan-survival controls. This filtered illumination is a laboratory test, not a claim that the early surface spectrum was benign. Supply natural pyrite independently; successful rxn_009 is not required.

reactions.mechanism: Photoexcited pyrite is proposed to couple imine reduction with sacrificial formate oxidation to carbon dioxide. Formate provides two electrons in the balanced net reaction; ammonia supplies the new amino nitrogen, and water is released.
reactions.reasoning: Analogue-supported but substrate-and-donor-system-unvalidated hypothesis. Li et al. (2024) demonstrate pyrite-associated photocatalytic reductive amination, including a low-yield aromatic example, but the supplied account does not establish this formate-fed indole-3-pyruvate system or the selected wavelength. Productive electron transfer must exceed direct and mineral-mediated indole photodestruction. The explicit spectrum and irradiance are proposed diagnostic variables, not reproduced published conditions.

reactions.name: Candidate Fe(II)-assisted transamination from glycine
agents: Dissolved Fe(II), introduced as FeCl2 in the laboratory screen

conditions.other: Proposed indole-3-pyruvate concentration 0.1-1 mM, glycine 10-100 mM, and dissolved Fe(II) 0.1-1 mM; pH 6.0-7.0; sample over 1-72 h. Exclude oxygen, UV, cyanide and sulfide. Verify dissolved versus precipitated iron rather than assuming a homogeneous catalyst. Use 15N-glycine in a diagnostic experiment and quantify both tryptophan and glyoxylate. No pyridoxal or enzyme is supplied.

reactions.mechanism: A productive metal-coordinated imine ensemble would transfer the amino group from glycine to the keto acid through proton rearrangement and hydrolysis. The net transformation is redox-neutral and produces glyoxylate. Formation and turnover of the required chelate remain hypotheses.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative donor-acceptor implementation. Ter-Ovanessian et al. (2025) support nonenzymatic amino-acid/keto-acid interconversion in related systems, not this glycine-to-indole-3-pyruvate pair or the proposed Fe(II) catalyst formulation. The explicit catalyst, pH and time window define a falsifiable test rather than an inferred working synthesis. Equilibrium position, slow amino transfer and acceptor decomposition are unresolved.

reactions.name: Candidate Fe(II)-assisted transamination from alanine
agents: Dissolved Fe(II), introduced as FeCl2 in the laboratory screen

conditions.other: Proposed indole-3-pyruvate concentration 0.1-1 mM, alanine 10-100 mM, and dissolved Fe(II) 0.1-1 mM; pH 6.0-7.0; sample over 1-72 h. Keep anoxic and shaded. Exclude cyanide and sulfide and measure iron speciation. Use 15N-alanine and quantify matched formation of tryptophan and pyruvate. No intrinsic superiority over glycine is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted imine formation, proton redistribution and hydrolysis would exchange the alanine amino group with the keto group of indole-3-pyruvate, releasing pyruvate. No external reductant is required by the net equation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative donor-acceptor implementation, with general nonenzymatic transamination context from Ter-Ovanessian et al. (2025). The supplied literature does not demonstrate this specific pair, establish an effective Fe(II) catalytic cycle or show favorable net conversion. Comparing alanine with glycine is chemically meaningful because the donor and keto-acid coproduct differ, but ranking the pathways requires measurements.

reactions.name: Glycolaldehyde Strecker entry to serine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed glycolaldehyde concentration 1-10 mM, total ammonia 50-200 mM, and total cyanide 5-50 mM; pH 8.0-9.0; residence time 1-48 h. Use a shaded, anoxic pool analogue. Quantify aminonitrile separately from cyanohydrin and sugar-derived products. A proposed laboratory cation-exchange fractionation and aqueous reconstitution must demonstrate recovery before transfer to rxn_014; natural fractionation remains unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde undergoes imine formation with ammonia and cyanide addition. Its hydroxymethyl group is retained, while cyanide introduces the carbon that becomes the serine carboxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Class-supported precursor chemistry consistent with the glycolaldehyde-Strecker serine module identified in the supplied report. The classical Strecker mechanism supports this connectivity (Strecker, 1850), but the stated numerical window and integration with tryptophan synthesis are proposed rather than established by the supplied findings. Competing cyanohydrin formation and carbonyl chemistry require quantitative assessment.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrolysis of serine aminonitrile
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline water; hydrolysis promoter

conditions.other: Proposed aminonitrile concentration 0.1-5 mM; initial pH at 298 K of 9.5-11.0; residence-time screen 6-168 h. Exclude oxygen and light. Cool to 303 K or below before solution conditioning. For rxn_015, use laboratory amino-acid isolation, desalting and reconstitution at pH 7-8; require measured free cyanide below 1 micromolar and low residual sulfide and iron. The cyanide limit is a proposed interference-control criterion, not a published inhibition threshold. Verify serine recovery and compare with untreated authentic serine.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydration followed by amide hydrolysis consumes two water molecules per aminonitrile and releases serine plus ammonia. The single mol_004 entry represents the inferred water coefficient of two.
reactions.reasoning: Class-supported Strecker completion, but neither the proposed hydrothermal window nor its integration with the terminal catalyst is demonstrated in the supplied research. Serine loss must be checked because nonenzymatic elimination and related amino-acid transformations are documented in adjacent chemistry (Ter-Ovanessian et al., 2025). Explicit isolation and cyanide testing address metal-catalyst compatibility without asserting a natural purification mechanism.

reactions.name: Pyridoxal-metal serine replacement: nonenzymatic laboratory benchmark
agents: Externally supplied Cu(II), introduced as CuCl2 and coordinated by pyridoxal and substrate

conditions.temperature: 363-373 K, proposed screen near the reported approximately 100 degrees Celsius model regime
conditions.other: Proposed concentrations: serine 10-50 mM, indole 0.1-1 mM, pyridoxal 0.5-2 mM and Cu(II) 0.05-0.2 mM; initial pH at 298 K of 7.0-8.0; residence-time screen 0.5-6 h. Keep anoxic and shaded. Use conditioned serine from rxn_014 only after recovery, cyanide and metal-compatibility checks. Exclude residual sulfide and strong reductants that could alter Cu(II) speciation. Include no-pyridoxal, no-metal and authentic-tryptophan survival controls. Exact substrate concentrations, catalyst loadings and pH are proposed, not extracted from the supplied paper.

reactions.mechanism: Pyridoxal forms a Schiff base with serine. Metal-assisted beta elimination generates a catalyst-bound aminoacrylate equivalent; indole attacks through C3, and hydrolysis releases tryptophan while regenerating pyridoxal. Water is the net coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Target-specific nonenzymatic reaction support: Metzler, Ikawa and Snell (1954; doi:10.1021/ja01632a004), also discussed by Newton and Snell (1964), establish tryptophan formation from serine and indole with pyridoxal-metal catalysis. This is the strongest demonstrated terminal chemistry in the network. However, the supplied report does not provide a complete reproducible formulation, and the numerical protocol here is a screening design rather than a claimed replication. Pyridoxal and the maintained copper formulation are external laboratory inputs with unresolved prebiotic availability; successful chemistry would not close that geochemical gap.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker route
pathways.description: Supplied indole-3-acetaldehyde enters Strecker chemistry and the aminonitrile undergoes alkaline hydrolysis. This is a conditional reaction-class-supported route, not an established synthesis from simple feedstocks. Aldehyde supply, hydrolysis rate and tryptophan survival remain gates.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-reservoir Strecker route
pathways.description: The supplied aldehyde is first trapped as a cyanohydrin, then equilibrated into the aminonitrile and hydrolyzed. This is a distinct entry sequence into the same terminal Strecker module, not independent evidence for target formation. Productive cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile flux must be measured.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker entry with hydantoin processing
pathways.description: The aminonitrile is trapped with inorganic carbon as a candidate hydantoin, followed by separate ring opening and carbamoyl hydrolysis. The indolic implementation is unvalidated, and downstream strong-base processing is explicitly a laboratory comparator rather than an established prebiotic setting.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin entry with hydantoin processing
pathways.description: Cyanohydrin equilibration supplies the same candidate hydantoin branch as P3. This is a distinct directed processing route, not a separate validated synthesis family. It inherits both the cyanohydrin-equilibrium uncertainty and the unvalidated indolic hydantoin hydrolyses.

pathways.name: Iron-hydroxide reductive amination
pathways.description: Supplied indole-3-pyruvate undergoes candidate reductive amination using consumable Fe(II) at a mixed-valence hydroxide interface. Related keto-acid experiments motivate the route, but neither this substrate nor the formal ferric product establishes productive kinetics.

pathways.name: Sulfide-to-pyrite coupled reductive amination
pathways.description: Supplied indole-3-pyruvate is paired with ammonia and a formal FeS/H2S reducing system. The central hypothesis is kinetic coupling of sulfur oxidation to imine reduction; pyrite formation without tryptophan would not validate the pathway.

pathways.name: Formate-fed pyrite photoreductive amination
pathways.description: A controlled illuminated pyrite system tests reduction of an indole-3-pyruvate-derived imine using formate as electron donor. Aromatic-keto-acid precedent is indirect, and the actual donor system, illumination window and competition with photodestruction remain unvalidated.

pathways.name: Glycine-donor transamination
pathways.description: Supplied indole-3-pyruvate receives an amino group from glycine in a proposed Fe(II)-assisted reaction, producing glyoxylate. This is a substrate-pair-specific research hypothesis, with explicit catalyst and isotope-tracing tests rather than assumed net conversion.

pathways.name: Alanine-donor transamination
pathways.description: Supplied indole-3-pyruvate receives an amino group from alanine in the proposed Fe(II) system, producing pyruvate. The donor and coproduct differ from P8, making this a distinct chemical route, but no relative yield or thermodynamic ranking is asserted.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde-to-serine module followed by the pyridoxal-metal benchmark
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde Strecker chemistry supplies serine aminonitrile, hydrolysis supplies serine, and a pyridoxal-metal system couples serine with supplied indole. The final transformation has direct nonenzymatic precedent. The integrated route still requires measured serine recovery, removal of catalyst-incompatible residues, indole availability and externally supplied pyridoxal-metal chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A chemically credible conditional route from the declared aldehyde feedstock. Strecker addition installs the correct tryptophan side-chain connectivity, and aminonitrile hydrolysis can furnish the target. The balance check establishes that rxn_002 requires two waters; there is no conservation violation. The principal uncertainties are aldehyde stability, hydrolysis rate versus decomposition, and the absence of an executable hydrothermal protocol. The supplied literature supports the reaction family rather than an integrated demonstration.
suggestions: Specify pH, temperature, pressure, residence time and concentrations for both steps.
Measure aldehyde and aminonitrile survival, authenticated tryptophan formation, and recovery during transfer and conditioning.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation and subsequent equilibration through aldehyde/imine chemistry provide a plausible route to the same aminonitrile. Describing rxn_004 as equilibration rather than direct displacement of hydroxide is chemically appropriate. However, neither a useful reservoir effect nor productive aminonitrile accumulation is established by the supplied evidence. The final hydrolysis has the same operational uncertainties as P1.
suggestions: Measure aldehyde, cyanohydrin and aminonitrile concentrations across ammonia concentration and pH.
Test whether cyanohydrin trapping improves recovered tryptophan production, including competing cyanohydrin hydrolysis and substrate degradation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin branch is structurally coherent and fully balanced. Aminonitrile conversion to a hydantoin is credible Bucherer–Bergs-type chemistry, followed by ring opening and decarbamoylation. Nevertheless, the supplied evidence does not establish this substrate-specific sequence or suitable surface conditions for rxn_005. Explicitly declaring strong-base processing as a laboratory comparator is appropriate; the remaining limitation is missing operating conditions and product-survival evidence, not the choice of laboratory reagents.
suggestions: Provide substrate-specific hydantoin references or experiments, including CO2 activity, pH and cyclization kinetics.
Confirm the hydantoin and N-carbamoyltryptophan structures, then measure selective hydrolysis and tryptophan recovery under specified base concentrations and temperatures.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a valid directed combination of the cyanohydrin-equilibration and hydantoin-processing modules. Its uncertainties concern productive equilibration, CO2-mediated cyclization and selective hydrolysis—not the number or order of steps. The proposed conditioning operations acknowledge compatibility problems but do not establish intermediate recovery or a working integrated procedure.
suggestions: Test hydantoin formation using the actual cyanohydrin/ammonia reaction mixture, with purified-aminonitrile controls.
Specify conditioning operations and quantify intermediate recovery, residual cyanide and tryptophan survival.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The reductive-amination connectivity is correct. Oxidation of two Fe(II) equivalents to Fe(III) supplies the required two electrons, consistent with the deterministic balance. Huber and Wächtershäuser (2003) and Barge et al. (2019) support related chemistry, but the supplied evidence does not demonstrate indole-3-pyruvate conversion. Pure Fe(OH)2 also cannot automatically be assigned the performance of Barge's mixed-valence precipitates. Substrate stability and mineral speciation remain decisive uncertainties.
suggestions: Specify mineral phase, Fe(II)/Fe(III) ratio, ammonia concentration, pH and temperature; compare pure and mixed-valence materials.
Measure tryptophan formation alongside indole-3-pyruvate loss and iron oxidation, using mineral-free and substrate-survival controls.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The equation is balanced, and oxidation of sulfide sulfur during pyrite formation can in principle provide reducing equivalents. However, favorable pyritization does not itself establish kinetic coupling to imine reduction. Related FeS-mediated reductive amination provides motivation, not direct evidence for this substrate and mineral-transformation mechanism. Competing hydrogen evolution, surface passivation and substrate degradation require assessment.
suggestions: Characterize starting and recovered mineral phases and measure pyrite formation and hydrogen production.
Compare FeS/H2S, preformed pyrite and hydrogen controls while quantifying authenticated tryptophan under defined sulfide activity and temperature.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Formate supplies a chemically appropriate net electron donor, and the equation conserves mass and charge. Li et al. (2024) support analogous pyrite photoreductive amination, including phenylpyruvate, but not the proposed indole-3-pyruvate/formate combination. The controlled-irradiation exception is consistent with the stated shielding policy. Missing illumination parameters, catalyst characterization and photostability measurements prevent stronger confidence. Pyrite need not appear as a consumed stoichiometric reactant.
suggestions: Document pyrite provenance or transfer, catalyst loading, wavelength, photon flux, pH and formate concentration.
Use dark, catalyst-free and donor-free controls, and measure both substrate and tryptophan photodegradation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glycine-to-glyoxylate transamination equation has correct connectivity and balance. General nonenzymatic transamination literature supports investigation, but does not establish useful Fe(II)-assisted transfer from glycine to indole-3-pyruvate. The equilibrium position, reaction rate, iron coordination state and competition with substrate degradation are unspecified. The pathway is a coherent hypothesis rather than demonstrated target production.
suggestions: Define Fe(II) loading, solution speciation, pH and temperature, including precipitation and metal-free controls.
Trace labeled glycine nitrogen into authenticated tryptophan and quantify glyoxylate formation with recovery controls.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Alanine can formally transfer its amino group to indole-3-pyruvate while becoming pyruvate, and the proposed equation is balanced. The supplied general metal-assisted transamination studies do not demonstrate this particular Fe(II)-assisted transformation. Reversibility, pyruvate accumulation and indole-3-pyruvate survival must be measured before assigning productive flux. No demonstrated advantage over the glycine-donor route is available.
suggestions: Measure forward and reverse reaction time courses across donor/acceptor ratios under explicitly defined iron conditions.
Use nitrogen-labeled alanine and quantify both tryptophan and pyruvate, distinguishing productive conversion from substrate disappearance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best-supported conditional laboratory route because rxn_015 has direct nonenzymatic experimental precedent with the stated substrates in Metzler, Ikawa and Snell (1954). The glycolaldehyde-to-serine module is also chemically credible. Accepting the explicitly supplied pyridoxal-metal catalyst does not establish a prebiotic process, but it does support chemical feasibility. Integrated production still requires serine survival during hydrolysis and control of cyanide/base carryover into metal catalysis. The specific catalytic protocol is absent.
suggestions: Specify the experimentally supported metal, pyridoxal loading and reaction conditions for rxn_015, with a reaction-level citation.
Measure serine recovery after hydrolysis and conditioning, then compare authentic serine with the actual upstream product mixture in the terminal reaction.

evaluation.network_feedback: Not approved at the 0.90 network threshold, although P1, P2 and P10 exceed the separate 0.80 pathway threshold. Structural validity is high: all 25 molecule nodes and 15 reaction nodes belong to one connected network, molecule IDs are consistent, and the listed pathways reach mol_025 from declared inputs. The deterministic check establishes zero mass or charge violations. Explicitly encode two waters in rxn_002 and rxn_014, and two equivalents each of ferrous hydroxide and ferric oxyhydroxide in rxn_008; these are modest coefficients, not chemical defects. Literature alignment is good in distinguishing demonstrated chemistry, substrate analogies, conditional hypotheses and laboratory comparators. The restriction of Wang et al. (2024) to irradiated ice chemistry is appropriate. Boundary feedstocks and laboratory catalysts are accepted on their declared terms; their unresolved natural availability limits geochemical conclusions rather than invalidating conditional synthesis. However, reaction-level citations are largely absent, the hydantoin branch lacks supporting references in the supplied research, and rxn_008 through rxn_012 remain substrate-specific extrapolations. Despite references to screening windows, the submitted reaction list contains no numerical operating protocols. Broad environment labels, shielding and anoxia therefore establish only partial environmental consistency. Transfer, fractionation and conditioning operations also lack specified procedures and measured recoveries. The strongest routes provide credible chemical access to tryptophan, but the complete network has not established compatible operating conditions, productive flux or target survival across its modules. Problematic-reaction flags identify evidential or operational gaps, not conservation failures.
